caption:
She never learned to read. She spent her childhood planting trees for a day's wage. She kept planting for 35 years before anyone noticed.

Tulsi Gowda was born into the Halakki tribal community in Honnalli, Karnataka, into extreme poverty with no access to formal education. From childhood she worked as a day-wage laborer alongside her mother, planting and tending saplings for a pittance. Her self-taught botanical knowledge - identifying tree species and 'mother trees' that no formally trained forester recognized - eventually led the Karnataka Forest Department to bring her on first as a volunteer, then permanently. Over roughly six decades she personally planted more than 30,000 saplings and her afforestation work strengthened one community reserve, five tiger reserves, fifteen conservation reserves and thirty wildlife sanctuaries. In 2021 she received the Padma Shri, India's fourth-highest civilian honor - a photo of her greeting dignitaries barefoot in her tribal attire became a widely shared symbol of grassroots dignity. She worked at the forest nursery until shortly before her death in December 2024, at about 86.
